t: Can Pop-Up Debate Produce Grit in Students?
q: My project will center around a series of 12 in-class “pop-up debates,” the final 10 of which will be filmed and uploaded as “link-only” files on YouTube for immediate student review. While I’ve already observed that these debates help students with content retention, speaking/listening skills, and argumentative ability, my hypothesis with this project is that debates can serve as a petri dish for grit as well.

It’s worth noting that the initial three weeks of T-P-S will also serve to normalize public speaking [1] (the S mode involves me randomly calling upon students for their now-rehearsed thoughts), thus helping to overcome one of the biggest barriers to having great pop-up debates: fear.

The key (unstated) objective for this debate is simple: I want kids to experience that standing up and speaking in front of their peers does not result in death; it’s scary, but not impossible. Nervousness isn’t cured, but it’s put in its place.

However, my hunch is that their growth is retarded by the simple fact that they aren't allowed immediate, adequate feedback on their performances. For example, they know that Palmer's Poise element involves removing distracting behaviors and verbal tics from one's speaking; however, many of them simply have no clue how guilty they still are at using “like, um, uh, you know” repetitively when they speak.

Video can solve this — everyone who has ever watched themselves on film shudders because it's brutal, unvarnished feedback. This is a critical component of deliberate practice, and deliberate practice is basically the thing that builds skill.

It requires mastering of content, attending to speech delivery, listening well, processing quickly, organizing one’s thinking, and being brave. In other words, it will serve as a source of consistent failure for all of my students, from lowest- to highest-achieving. This failure will provide fertile soil for the Grit Tips, which will be designed for immediate application.

I have three years experience with scaffolding students toward successfully participating in Debate 1. The first debate is a pivotal moment, as students learn, “Hey, I can do this; it’s nerve-wracking, but I can do it.” Of the 200 students I’ve taught in the past three years, exactly one has refused to participate.
x: The hypothesis is that a debate can serve as a petri dish for grit, not just for argument - a claim Stuart proposes to test with filmed evidence rather than assert.
The sequencing is the transferable part: three weeks of think-pair-share to normalize public speaking before Debate 1, because fear is the biggest barrier to a working pop-up debate.

Video is justified as deliberate practice with a 24 Hour Rule, on the grounds that students who know Palmer's Poise element still have no idea how often they say 'like, um, uh, you know.'.

Video is his answer to the missing ingredient in their growth: students believe they have poise until footage shows them their own verbal tics, and unvarnished feedback is what deliberate practice requires.
His theory of why this should work is unusually candid - pop-up debate is hard enough to guarantee failure for every student, top to bottom, and that failure is the fertile soil the Grit Tips need.
Pairing each debate with both a Target Skill and a Grit Tip, each on its own notebook page, gives students something to execute and something to practice at the same time.

t: What Effective Classroom Management Really Means ly-means/
q: For many teachers, effective classroom management brings to mind an image of a silent, somber environment.
Effective classroom management isn’t a no-fun, you-against-them proposition. It isn’t a dampening or suppressing of behavior. And it isn’t uptight, tense, or stressful.
It’s about trust and influence. It’s about relationships and leadership. It’s about students behaving and giving their best because they want to, not because they’re forced to.
It includes strictness only in a sense that well-defined boundaries of behavior—whose only goal is to protect learning and enjoyment—are faithfully maintained.
Simply put, effective classroom management is where the desires and fulfillment of both students and teachers meet.
We’ve heard from hundreds of teachers just like you who have put our simple and honest strategies into action and experienced transformational results.
x: For students this means freedom to thrive academically and build friendships without bullying; for teachers it means freedom to teach without constant interference.
Effective classroom management is reframed away from the common image of a silent, restrictive, disciplinarian environment.
Linsin defines it instead as a collection of gentle but powerful strategies built on trust, relationships, and leadership, where students behave because they want to.
Well-defined behavioral boundaries exist to protect learning and enjoyment, and within them lies genuine freedom for both students and teachers.
Effective classroom management is reframed away from the common image of a silent, restrictive, disciplinarian environment.
The article positions this definition as achievable for any teacher, regardless of school context or student population, citing testimonials from teachers who applied SCM's strategies.

t: What Are the Keystone Habits for Success?
q: The best teachers give themselves the freedom to form and test hypotheses that could be wrong. They have hunches that they act on.

When we enter into a political debate, for example, with our mind resolutely made up and our identity staked on our claim, we are highly unlikely to leave that debate with any kind of greater understanding or clarity. Our main takeaway will be: they are wrong; I am right. It seems we've discussed the issues, but actually we've just taken turns with target practice.

When we enter a decision with our mind already made up, the same is true: we'll leave with a “decision,” but it's unlikely that we've made the best one. We've used a biased scale to weigh out the options, ending up exactly where we wanted to. This is a huge deal if we want to lead a flourishing life and help our students do likewise.

I suspect that habits are a key part of the picture for increasing the success of our kids. Many of my kids leave class inspired by their progress and their visions for their futures, yet only those who have developed successful habits tend to do anything with that inspiration.
Inspiration is not enough in our classrooms, my colleagues. It leads to short-term bursts of energy; it facilitates joy; it's beautiful and it's part of why I love this work.

q: Trying and failing to motivate unmotivated students is a common frustration among teachers.
True motivation, however—that which is internal and sustaining—doesn’t develop through convincing. It isn’t about ramped-up enthusiasm or flattery.
The first step is to stop the flow of excessive and over-the-top praise.
You’re going to give plain and honest feedback about the evidence you see on the page or screen.
Now, it’s important to note that it must be true. The least motivated in particular can recognize phoniness from a mile a way.
By truthfully pointing out quality when you see it, you spark their once dormant intrinsic motivational engine to life. You wake up the sleeping giant.
x: Standard motivational advice—praise, encouragement, reward, repeat—is described as largely ineffective with chronically unmotivated students.
True, lasting motivation is framed as intrinsic inspiration rather than something achieved by external convincing or cheerleading.
Step one of the strategy: stop excessive praise, pep-talks, and 'talking students through' their capabilities.
Step two: quietly watch for genuine evidence of quality work and respond with plain, honest, specific observations about the work itself, delivered without an exaggerated tone.
Michael Linsin proposes a strategy for reaching chronically unmotivated students that departs from the usual advice of increased praise, encouragement, and pep talks.

t: Keystone Habits: Unlocking Success for our Students and Ourselves
q: I teach fourteen-year-olds that I genuinely love, but that doesn't mean their actions don't often frustrate me. I've got my fair share of “Wow, these kids are amazing” stories from this year's crop of kids (and every crop before), but I'm much more intensely interested in why they don't do as well as I hope they will.

I commend a third way: super grounded in a balanced reality. In general, we ought to strive for a view of students that is fervently committed to their potential for long-term flourishing and therefore relentlessly facing the brutal facts so that we can make adjustments toward what works.

The majority of my students who don't do their homework do not lack the desire to be successful. The problem is that, even though they are visualizing in class how and when they'll do their homework, that visualization doesn't succeed against their home-from-school routines.

It's the same reason that many of my students don't do their homework! Success in school is like being physically fit — it requires this whole set of tiny behaviors to happen on a consistent basis, day in and day out.

The good news is that researchers have found that not all habits are equal. For example, with physical fitness, they've found that if you just develop one small habit, the rest are much more likely to follow — that one small habit is exercising for a few minutes a day.
So the question is, how do we help students change their habits? How do we help ourselves change our habits to do the things we've always dreamed about doing?

It makes me wonder: what are the keystone habits of thinking, reading, writing, and speaking? What's the keystone habit of developing things like grit and self-control? I'll be talking more about that lattermost bit in the weeks to come, as I have a very fun announcement to make next week.
x: Dave Stuart Jr. uses Charles Duhigg's The Power of Habit to ask why his ninth graders fail to do homework they genuinely intend to do.
Stuart rejects both rosy and negative views of students in favor of a grounded realism that faces brutal facts in service of long-term flourishing.
Missing homework is diagnosed as a habit problem rather than a motivation problem: students' visualized plans lose to the cue-routine-reward loop of home-from-school routines.
Success in school is compared to physical fitness, both requiring many tiny behaviors repeated consistently, which explains why so many people want them yet lack them.
He then draws a parallel to his own struggles with physical fitness and introduces the keystone habit, a single small behavior that sets off a cascade of further changes.
He frames the open question for teachers as identifying the keystone habits of reading, writing, speaking, grit and self-control.

q: The good news is that as long as it was a minor setback, and not a total loss of control, it isn’t difficult to do.
When recovering from a bad day, lining up outside will also send the message that the expectation bar has been picked up off the floor and placed back on the top rung where it belongs.
Rehashing yesterday’s woes is counterproductive. It merely drags the bad energy with you into the morning.
The first routine of the day is critical in restoring your classroom to its well-behaved state. A smooth and efficient performance will put to rest any concerns from the day before.
The biggest mistake teachers make after a bad day is to turn grim and standoffish, to use a show of disappointment and the threat of turning ‘mean’ as a hedge against a repeat performance.
The steps above, however, address the cause of the problems from the day before. They refresh and restore your classroom back to well-being.

t: How To Handle Class-Clown Disruptions And Disrespect -disrespect/
q: The truth is, the most effective classrooms laugh. They laugh and joke and enjoy each other much more than most teachers realize.
But an angry reaction will only make matters worse. It will extend and deepen the interruption. It will bring stress and negativity into your classroom.
The truth is, when they make a silly comment, their intention isn’t to humiliate you. How you feel about it emotionally isn’t even on their radar.
Reacting in anger won’t cut it, not even close. In fact, the most effective reaction is no reaction at all.
You see, when you let the elephant in the room just stand there, alone and awkward and shuffling its feet, the lesson becomes powerful and meaningful to everyone in the class.
In less than 60 seconds you’re back to work. As if it never happened.
x: Humor is framed as a genuine potential asset in the classroom, and the most effective classrooms are described as ones that laugh and enjoy each other, within the bounds of class rules.
An angry reaction to a disruptive joke is said to worsen the disruption, extend the interruption, and damage the teacher-student relationship long-term.
Disruptive jokes or comments that pull the class off task are usually motivated by a student's desire to entertain peers, not to humiliate the teacher personally.
Instead, Linsin recommends what he calls the most effective reaction.
